newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: US brushes off reports of trade tension with LatAm.
newsitem.headline: US brushes off reports of trade tension with LatAm.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley Friday played down reports of tensions in free trade talks with Latin America, calling them differences on "wording" and saying there was plenty of time to solve them.
"There will be a lot of fighting over the language, obviously, and debate and discussions over the language of different wordings," Daley told reporters.

He said he could not confirm reports out of Belo Horizonte, Brazil, that U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky earlier in the day threatened to "pack our bags and go home" after alleged differences with other regional nations during free trade discussions.
"The conversations that I had there were positive," said Daley, who earlier in the week participated in the Belo Horizonte talks aimed at setting up a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).

The secretary said he would be "surprised" if they did not agree on the "need to move forward". He put down part of the controversy to what he said were exaggerated expectations that there would be substantial negotiations in Belo Horizonte.
"The most important (round of negotiations) is Santiago in March of 1998," he said referring to the pan-American presidential summit planned in the Chilean capital next year.

Ministers attending the Belo Horizonte talks said the main sticking point was Washington's insistence on pushing for free trade at full speed, while South America's Mercosur trade bloc of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay was advocating caution.
But Daley said the target for formally launching FTAA was 2005, which left plenty of room for ironing out differences.
"We know this is a very long process," he said.

Launched at a summit of 34 nations from the Americas in 1994 in Miami, the FTAA envisages setting up a free trade zone of nearly one billion consumers with a combined gross domestic product of over $9.0 trillion.

According to a Portuguese translation of her address to the meeting in Belo Horizonte, Barshefsky said: "This declaration is inconsistent with what happened in Miami. We are trying to rewrite Miami and this cannot be agreed to by the United States."
Participants said that while Mercosur wants to negotiate in stages, with tariff custs left until last, Washington wanted to discuss everything from tariffs to subsidies at the same time.

Ministers in Belo Horizonte were also discussing whether to give the labor movement a bigger say in the negotiating process, with some delegates reportedly taking issue with Brazil's distribution of a "Manifesto of the Workers of the Americas" hammered out by trade unions earlier in the week.
"We have no problem with that at all," Daley said. "The business and labor communities should he consulted and their recommendations put forward."
He said the United States included labor and environmental issues when it negotiated the NAFTA free trade deal with Canada and Mexico.
